DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
Timely Petition for Review having been filed by the Petitioner herein and notice given to 
all parties, the Commission, after considering the issues of accident, employment, causal 
connection, and temporary total disability, and being advised of the facts and law, affirms and 
adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which is attached hereto and made a part hereof.   
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed September 25, 2025 is hereby affirmed and adopted. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Respondent pay to 
Petitioner interest under §19(n) of the Act, if any. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Respondent shall have 
credit for all amounts paid, if any, to or on behalf of the Petitioner on account of said accidental 
injury. 
Based upon the denial of compensation herein, no bond is set by the Commission. The 
party commencing the proceedings for review in the Circuit Court shall file with the Commission 
a Notice of Intent to File for Review in Circuit Court.

Tylor, Anthony 
Case # 25 WC 005100 
Employee/Petitioner 
 
v. 
  
 
We Clean Carpet, Inc. 
Employer/Respondent 
 
An Application for Adjustment of Claim was filed in this matter, and a Notice of Hearing was mailed to each 
party.  The matter was heard by the Honorable Jacqueline Hickey, Arbitrator of the Commission, in the city 
of Chicago, on June 26, 2025.  After reviewing all of the evidence presented, the Arbitrator hereby makes 
findings on the disputed issues checked below and attaches those findings to this document. 
 
DISPUTED ISSUES 
 
A. 
 Was Respondent operating under and subject to the Illinois Workers' Compensation or Occupational  
 
 Diseases Act? 
 
B. 
 Was there an employee-employer relationship? 
 
C. 
 Did an accident occur that arose out of and in the course of Petitioner's employment by Respondent? 
 
D. 
 What was the date of the accident? 
 
E. 
 Was timely notice of the accident given to Respondent? 
 
F. 
 Is Petitioner's current condition of ill-being causally related to the injury? 
 
G. 
 What were Petitioner's earnings? 
 
H. 
 What was Petitioner's age at the time of the accident? 
 
I. 
 What was Petitioner's marital status at the time of the accident? 
 
J. 
 Were the medical services that were provided to Petitioner reasonable and necessary?  Has Respondent  
 paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services? 
 
K. 
 Is Petitioner entitled to any prospective medical care? 
 
L. 
 What temporary benefits are in dispute?   
 
 
 TPD  
 Maintenance 
 TTD 
 
M. 
 Should penalties or fees be imposed upon Respondent? 
 
N. 
 Is Respondent due any credit? 
 
O. 
 Other  Nature and Extent

FINDINGS 
 
On the date of accident, 2/14/2025, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions of the Act.   
 
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did not exist between Petitioner and Respondent.   
 
On this date, Petitioner did not sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment. 
 
Timely notice of this accident was given to Respondent. 
 
Petitioner's current condition of ill-being is not causally related to the accident. 
 
In the week preceding the injury, Petitioner earned N/A, Petitioner was a new hire; the average weekly wage 
was approximately $342.00 based on the evidence. 
 
On the date of accident, Petitioner was 39 years of age, single with 1 dependent child. 
 
Respondent has not paid all reasonable and necessary charges for all reasonable and necessary medical 
services.   
 
Respondent shall be given a credit of $ N/A for TTD, $ N/A for TPD, $ N/A for maintenance, and $ N/A for 
other benefits, for a total credit of $ 0.00. 
 
Respondent is entitled to a credit of $0 under Section 8(j) of the Act. 
 
ORDER 
 
The petitioner’s claim for benefits is hereby denied as further explained below and in the Rider to Decision: 
 
• The Arbitrator finds that an employee-employer relationship did not exist between Petitioner and 
Respondent on the date of alleged accident.  
• The Arbitrator finds that Petitioner did not sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of 
employment because Petitioner was not employed by Respondent on the date of the alleged accident.  
 
RULES REGARDING APPEALS  Unless a party files a Petition for Review within 30 days after receipt of this 
decision, and perfects a review in accordance with the Act and Rules, then this decision shall be entered as the 
decision of the Commission.   
STATEMENT OF INTEREST RATE  If the Commission reviews this award, interest at the rate set forth on the Notice 
of Decision of Arbitrator shall accrue from the date listed below to the day before the date of payment; 
however, if an employee's appeal results in either no change or a decrease in this award, interest shall not 
accrue.

RIDER TO DECISION  
This matter proceeded to hearing on June 26, 2025 before Arbitrator Jacqueline Hickey on 
Petitioner’s Petition for Immediate Hearing pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Act. Issues in dispute 
include: employee-employer relationship, accident, causal connection, AWW, TTD benefits, 
medical bills, and nature and extent. See Arbitrator’s Exhibit 1 (“Ax1”). At trial, Petitioner’s 
Exhibits A-H and Respondent’s Exhibits 1 and 3 were admitted into evidence.  
 
FINDINGS OF FACT 
Testimony of Anthony Tylor 
The petitioner, Mr. Anthony Tylor, is a 40-year-old male formerly employed with We Clean 
Carpet as a Carpet Cleaning Technician. Petitioner testified he began working for respondent when 
he was 15 years old and was introduced to respondent by his cousin, Jason. (Tr. 11). He worked 
there on and off for about six or seven years and was rehired in 2025, but did not remember who 
hired him. (Tr. 12-14). The stip sheet lists an accident date of February 14, 2025 and accident is 
disputed by Respondent (Ax1).  
 
Petitioner reported that he was given a company vehicle to use for travel to jobs along with 
company issued equipment and carpet cleaning supplies. (Tr. 15). He further stated that shortly 
after starting with respondent he was assigned training with another employee, Mr. Benjamin 
Worcester, to get familiar with company procedures. (Tr. 16). Petitioner testified that part of his 
training involved “upsales” to customers. Petitioner described these extra sales offers as soap, 
deodorizer, Scotch guard, or sanitizer. (Tr. 17). He stated that if an “upsale” was not made at a job 
site, he would be flagged in the computer system, which would result in a phone call with someone 
from the respondent, but did not recall who exactly.   
 
 
26IWCC0137

2 
 
Petitioner testified that he spent three- or four-days training with Mr. Worcester and that they used 
a company vehicle, which he was allowed to take home each night. (Tr. 19). Petitioner reported 
that the accident occurred on February 14, 2025. (Tr. 20). Petitioner stated that he would do at 
least four jobs a day in the days leading up to the accident but would occasionally do more. (Tr. 
21). 
 
Regarding wages, Petitioner stated that he was never given a pay scale and never discussed 
compensation with anyone from the respondent. (See PxE). His expectation was that he would 
make between $1,000.00 and $1,200.00 per week because respondent knew his cousin. (Tr. 22). 
Petitioner reported that he was told by someone at respondent that his compensation would make 
$150.00 per day training with Worcester and that he was never shown anything in writing 
regarding a pay scale. (Tr. 92). Petitioner stated that he was told he would be paid up to $1,218.00 
weekly. (Tr. 95).  
 
Petitioner testified that he had no idea that he was terminated from respondent prior to the alleged 
accident date of February 14, 2025. (Tr. 23). He stated he would typically work six days a week 
and had worked the days leading up to the 14th including the 12th and 13th of February. (Tr. 23). 
 
Petitioner stated that on the day of the accident, he had the company vehicle at his home and was 
waiting for a job assignment. He reported that jobs were assigned from respondent via cellphone 
and would include an address and the details of the services that were requested. (Tr. 25). On the 
morning of February 14, 2025, petitioner stated he got a call from his co-worker, Benjamin 
Worcester, stating he needed roadside assistance due to his vehicle being down.   Petitioner 
testified that Worcester’s vehicle had a prior history of needing roadside assistance. (Tr. 26).  
 
Petitioner stated that there were special safety features within the company vehicle, including a 
need for approval from respondent before the vehicle could start. A signal would need to be sent 
from the respondent to an “App” before the vehicle could be used.  If the driver tried to turn on 
the vehicle without approval, it would not start. Petitioner testified that once the vehicle was on, it 
would not shut down until the vehicle was turned off. (Tr. 28 & 29). 
 
On the date of the accident, petitioner testified he informed the respondent of his intentions to go 
to Mr. Worcester’s house to assist him with his vehicle. He stated he let someone from 
respondent’s office know of his intentions for the trip and was authorized to do so. (Tr. 31). 
Petitioner testified that he could not remember whom he spoke with from respondent.  (Tr. 31).  
Petitioner stated that he believed Mr. Worcester was in higher position than himself because he 
was asked to train petitioner. (Tr. 81). On the date of the accident, petitioner reported speaking 
with Mr. Worcester around six or seven in the morning when he was at his mother’s house at 9950 
Emerald Avenue. (Tr. 81). Petitioner left the Emerald address around 8:00AM to go to Mr. 
Worcester’s home.  (Tr. 83). Petitioner then stated he was going to a job before being rerouted to 
Mr. Worcester ’s house. (Tr. 84).Petitioner was familiar with where Mr. Worcester lived and had 
been there before.  
 
 
 
26IWCC0137

3 
 
He reported that he entered the 290 expressway and was struck from behind by another vehicle 
causing him to hit the vehicle in front of him. (Tr. 32). He described the hit as “heavy,” before 
getting out of the vehicle and speaking with one of the other drivers involved in the accident. (Tr. 
33). He reported one of the other drivers left the scene before he was able to call the police, who 
then directed the parties to get off the highway and go to a gas station.  (Tr. 34). At that time, 
petitioner testified that a police report was made. Petitioner stated that he informed respondent of 
the accident, provided photos, and was told to go pick up Mr. Worcester and continue with the 
workday. Petitioner again testified he could not recall whom he spoke with from respondent at the 
time of this reporting. (Id.)  
 
Petitioner reported that he drove 18 minutes to Mr. Worcester’s home. (Tr. 37). Petitioner stated 
he and Worcester completed two or three jobs that afternoon he dropped Mr. Worcester off at 
8:00PM. (Tr. 38).  Petitioner testified he dropped Mr. Worcester off at home, then got stuck in a 
storm and did not get home until late. (Tr. 91). He stated he woke up the next day with head and 
back pain. (Tr. 39). Petitioner testified he had a back injury several years prior, with eight or nine 
months of physical therapy. (Tr. 41). 
 
Petitioner testified that on February 15, 2025, he received a call from respondent, though he could 
not recall exactly whom.  During that call, petitioner stated he was ready to work.  Petitioner 
testified that respondent told him to take his damaged work vehicle into a mechanic shop on 
Loomis for an estimate. (Tr. 42; 88). Petitioner stated that he took the vehicle into the requested 
auto shop but was sent to another shop as they were unable to complete the requested work.  
Petitioner testified that he let someone from the respondent’s office know that he was taking the 
vehicle to another shop and that he believed this was approved because the work vehicle was 
allowed to turn on. (Tr. 43; 100). He reported that he had the vehicle turned on by someone from 
respondent’s office, but then went to the emergency room instead as his body began to ache. (Tr. 
44).   
 
The Arbitrator notes that when asked on cross-examination if at any time, he had disabled the 
security features in the company vehicle, petitioner stated he had not. (Tr. 92). 
 
Petitioner first sought treatment at Northwestern ER on February 15, 2025, where he underwent 
x-rays and was discharged with instructions to follow up with his doctor. (Tr. 45).  Petitioner 
reported he drove the company vehicle on February 15, 2025 to the Garfield Park Police Station 
to follow up. When he went to start the vehicle to leave, he was not given authority by respondent 
and was unable to operate it. He reported that he was told he would be ordered an Uber, but never 
was. (Tr. 49). He then sent photos of the vehicle to respondent to let them know where they could 
get the vehicle. (Tr. 49). Petitioner testified that he then provided doctor notes to respondent letting 
them know how he was feeling and was never made aware that he was terminated at any point. 
(Tr. 50). 
 
Petitioner testified that he went back to Northwestern maybe five or six days after the accident as 
he was feeling some pain. (Tr. 51). He reported having nerve issues causing incontinence. He then 
followed up with Doctores de Accidentes, where he attended physical therapy. (Tr. 52). Petitioner 
was then referred to a neurologist and referenced pain on the back of his head, which he stated was 
caused by striking the back of a shelf in the work vehicle during the accident. (Tr. 55).  
26IWCC0137

4 
 
Petitioner described suffering from headaches that go in and out with random throbbing. They had 
gotten somewhat better since February 2025, but he had not been symptom free. (Tr. 57). He was 
referred to a pain specialist, Chicago Pain and Rehab, from Doctores de Accidentes. While at 
Chicago Pain, petitioner underwent six injections to his spine. (Tr. 58). The injections helped with 
the pain, but did not take it all away or cure his incontinence issues. (Tr. 58). He reported receiving 
an off work note from his doctor on February 17, 2025, that took him off work until June 17, 2025. 
(Tr. 61). 
 
At trial, petitioner reported that he still has back pain that affects his ability to sleep. He rated his 
lower back pain a six or seven our of ten, worsening at night. (Tr. 66).  Petitioner reported that he 
last sought treatment for his injuries, a few days before trial. He also has pending appointments for 
therapy and injections. (Tr. 97). 
 
When asked how many jobs he worked per day for respondent, petitioner stated that he would 
work four jobs a day, six days a week. He first testified that he only worked for respondent for a 
few days. (Tr. 77). He later stated he worked there several weeks. (Tr. 78). Petitioner stated he was 
never made aware of any complaints against him from customers during his tenure with 
respondent. (Tr. 78). He also stated that he was never made aware he was terminated at any point 
and that he was never asked by respondent to return his work vehicle on February 13, 2025. (Tr. 
79). 
 
Petitioner reported he never received a paycheck from respondent.  He received gas 
reimbursement. (Tr. 61). He also stated that he was told after the accident that his pay would go 
towards the damages to the work vehicle. (Id.) 
 
Petitioner reported that he has not heard from respondent and has not worked any other jobs for 
the company since February 14, 2025. He testified that he has been off work since that time (Tr. 
69). 
 
Petitioner testified that he used to have a proprietorship called Demolition Expert, but that he had 
not worked under it for years. He also worked for Tylor Construction in the past, years ago. (Tr. 
76). Finally, he reported working for a roadside assistance business named Presidential Towing 
years ago. (Tr. 77). 
 
Testimony of Benjamin Worcester   
Benjamin Worcester testified that he was a former employee of the respondent. He stated that after 
14 years of employment with respondent, he was terminated after an auto collision with the 
company vehicle (Tr. 104). He reported he was terminated February 26, 2025, the day after his 
accident. (Tr. 105). He also stated that he was terminated prior and brought back after two months 
due to a pay restructuring. (Tr. 105). 
 
Mr. Worcester first reported meeting petitioner in February 2025 as a new trainee. (Tr. 107). 
Petitioner would drive to his home and he would show petitioner how to complete jobs and make 
“upsales” to customers. (Tr. 108).  Mr. Worcester stated that if you fail to “upsell” a customer, you 
would be barred from receiving another job until a conversation occurred with respondent’s 
office.(Id.)  
26IWCC0137

5 
 
Mr. Worcester testified that job assignment was all done via an “App” installed on either a phone 
or company supplied tablet. (Tr. 108). He stated that he would bring the company vehicle home 
every night and every morning.  He would then request a job before the vehicle would be able to 
be turned on. (Tr. 111). Mr. Worcester testified that the work vehicle had four cameras and GPS 
tracking. (Tr. 113). 
 
Mr. Worcester stated that his company vehicle started having issues prior to February 14, 2025, 
and that respondent was aware. (Tr. 114). On the day of the accident, he reported that his vehicle 
would not start, so he called petitioner to come assist him. (Tr. 116). Mr. Worcester testified that 
he was not aware if petitioner was terminated on February 14, 2025 and “no one ever said he was 
fired to me”. (Tr. 117). 
 
Mr. Worcester testified that he did not become aware of petitioner’s accident until petitioner 
arrived at his home on February 14, 2025, and he could see the damage to the vehicle.  (Tr. 118). 
Upon arrival, they loaded the gear from Mr. Worcester’s vehicle to petitioner’s vehicle and went 
to complete two or three more jobs. (Tr. 119). He stated that they were able to complete the 
additional jobs despite petitioner complaining of headaches. He further explained that petitioner 
seemed a bit off, weaker, and that he had to assist with most of the heavy lifting. (Tr. 120). 
According to Mr. Worcester, respondent was aware that they were completing jobs after the 
accident. (Tr. 121). He learned that petitioner was terminated on the 15th. (Tr. 121). 
 
Mr. Worcester testified that it was normal for employees to be terminated after they were involved 
in an accident. He also stated employees would be charged for missing or damaged equipment. 
(Tr. 124). He reported his title was the same as petitioner’s and he had the same pay scale as every 
other cleaning technician. (Tr. 126). He clarified that pay would vary depending on season, but an 
average check would be between $700.00 and $1,000.00. (Tr. 127). He stated technicians were 
required to complete four jobs a day, six days a week. (Tr. 131). 
 
On cross-examination, Mr. Worcester testified that he was employed as a cleaning technician and 
never had a position of authority like manager or supervisor. (Tr. 132). He reported that he received 
jobs the same way as other technicians and he did not assign jobs. (Tr. 133). The only time he 
directed other technicians was during training, when figuring out where to meet up before going 
to a job. (Tr. 133). Mr. Worcester confirmed that he last worked for respondent on February 26, 
2025 and has no current relationship with the company. He is currently doing medicine delivery, 
which he started two weeks ago. (Tr. 134). 
 
Mr. Worcester testified that on the date of the accident, he spoke with petitioner and Mr. John 
Allgood from the respondent around 7:00AM. Petitioner let him know that he was getting ready 
for a job. (Tr. 135).  Mr. Worcester previously testified that he messaged with Allgood, and 
informed him that petitioner was going to come assist him with his broken vehicle. (Tr. 117 and 
136). According to Worcester, he texted Allgood at 10:39AM and received a response around 
12:00PM or 1:00PM, and that they completed two or three jobs that day. (Tr. 137).  
 
 
 
26IWCC0137

6 
 
Mr. Worcester testified that he was not made aware that petitioner was terminated. (Tr. 137). When 
asked what he was told by Mr. Allgood on 2/14/25 after reporting his work van issues he testified 
“he said that the gentleman is coming out and I told him to make sure he removes the manager’s 
button.” (Tr. 136) Mr. Worcester testified that “they knew he was coming out” because “he also 
removed the manager button sign on my phone”. (Tr.117).  
 
Testimony of Jonathan Allgood 
Jonathan Allgood testified that he is employed as the Service Manager for We Clean Carpet. (Tr. 
142). He has been employed with respondent for 14 years and stated that they have been in business 
since 2011. (Tr. 142). At trial, Mr. Allgood identified a screenshot of his service manager software. 
(RX 1). He explained that this software gives him information on all technicians employed with 
respondent. The software allows him to see what their assignments are, see any infractions, and 
attendance points. Mr. Allgood likened the software to a personnel file for each technician. (Tr. 
144). He testified that he is the only person with access to these files and stated that he reviews 
them in the ordinary course of business. (Tr. 144). 
 
Mr. Allgood described his job duties as handling customer relations, including equipment and 
vehicle repairs. Allgood testified that petitioner was hired on January 30, 2025, as a cleaning 
technician and that all technicians are provided with a work vehicle that they are allowed to take 
home with them at night. (Tr. 146). Each vehicle is equipped with GPS tracking, front-facing and 
rear-facing dash cameras, and a starter-disabler that prevents the vehicle from being started without 
permission from the company. These are installed behind plastic molding in the vehicle. (Tr. 146). 
 
Mr. Allgood testified that compensation for all cleaning technicians is the same, and they are paid 
on commission based on the work that is done. Every technician gets 20 percent of each dispatched 
job and up to 50 percent of any additional services they provide to the customer. (Tr. 147).  Each 
dispatch is charged $89.00, and each technician would receive 20 percent of this cost. Technicians 
complete around three jobs a day on average. (Tr. 147). He also described the “upsale” process.   
Mr. Allgood stated that technicians go out to the job site, review, and provide an estimate for 
requested services. (Tr. 148). The technicians go into the job knowing what services are requested, 
but not the extent of the cleaning needed, so part of their job is to review the situation and provide 
an accurate quote with appropriate supplies. (Tr. 148). 
 
Mr. Allgood testified that technicians were required to work six days a week, Monday through 
Saturday, and the goal was to complete 24 jobs a week.  Most would complete between 18 and 20 
jobs per week. (Tr. 150). He reported that petitioner only worked a total of four days, outside of 
training, and the amount earned per day was $40.00. (Tr. 150). 
 
Mr. Allgood testified that in order to use the work vehicle, a technician needed to have an 
assignment, which was automatically done through software (the “App”) where the technicians 
were assigned a job and given directions. He stated this was an automated process and there was 
no direct communication with the company when getting job assignments. (Tr. 152). Once given 
a job assignment, directions would populate, and the technician would be able to start the vehicle. 
(Tr. 152). When it came to GPS tracking, respondent would be notified if technicians drove off 
the designated route. (Tr. 153). 
26IWCC0137

7 
 
Mr. Allgood testified that petitioner was to start work on January 30, 2025. Petitioner was 
contacted five times by the dispatcher regarding his start, but he never responded, so respondent 
assumed he was not interested in working for them. (Tr. 154). Petitioner was then subsequently 
re-hired on February 8, 2025 and given job assignments.  Mr. Allgood testified that petitioner 
worked five jobs for respondent before he was terminated on February 12, 2025. (Tr. 209).  
 
Mr. Allgood testified that customers would call in requested services to respondent.  After 
contacting respondent, customers would be quoted the requested services by the technician. If a 
quote was not provided, the request would be flagged.  (Tr. 156). There is also a button that can 
be pressed within the App indicating that a quote was provided, but the customer declined service. 
(Tr. 157). 
 
When asked about a February 10, 2025 date in the service manager screenshot, Mr. Allgood 
explained that the notation of “another voicemail” was automatically populated because a 
customer had called in the previous day to complain. (Tr. 157). (RX 1). He recalled that the 
February 10, 2025 voicemail was from a customer that complained about the quality of work done 
by petitioner.  This customer wanted a technician to come back to address the job.  (Tr. 158). Mr. 
Allgood testified that after receiving the February 10, 2025 customer complaint, he addressed it 
directly with petitioner. (Id.) 
 
At trial, Mr. Allgood next reviewed each note associated with the February 11, 2025 date in the 
service manager screenshot. (Tr. 159). (RX 1). The first note stated, “quota talk, 6.00 average 
upsell per room”. Mr. Allgood explained that this meant that the target amount of money petitioner 
was supposed to bring in from a job was significantly less than expected. As a result, he testified 
that petitioner would need to be retrained on upsales. (Tr. 160). The next note from February 11, 
2025 was “truck idling more than 30 minutes”. This meant that the tracking device in the 
petitoiner’s work vehicle showed the vehicle idling for more than 30 minutes, which is against 
company policy. (Tr. 160-161). Mr. Allgood reviewed a third note from February 11, 2025 listed 
as “did not get paid in time”. He explained that when the technician is within range of the 
customers house, verified by GPS, they have 45 minutes to get the customers signature. The 
average time for obtaining the customer signature is eight minutes. (Tr. 161). On February 11, 
2025, petitioner was flagged for not completing this step in a timely fashion. (Tr. 162). Mr. Allgood 
testified about a fourth note associated with petitioner’s services on February 11, 2025. He stated 
that this was another voicemail came in with a complaint from a customer.  (Tr. 162). Mr. Allgood 
testified that respondent had to refund the customer due to petitioner’s poor work.  (Tr. 162). The 
final note from February 11, 2025 was reviewed by Mr. Allgood, which stated “TU 3, not happy 
with cleaning, sent bad review, asked for us to call him”. He further explained this note reflected 
another customer complaint regarding petitioner’s work product. (Tr. 163). The “TU” stands for 
“touch up”, which Allgood stated directs a technician to go back to a job and address any 
complaints. (Tr. 164). Mr. Allgood testified that this amount of customer complaints regarding a 
particular technician in as short period of time was unusual.  (Tr. 164). 
 
 
 
 
26IWCC0137

8 
 
On February 12, 2025, Mr. Allgood explained that there was another voicemail complaint 
regarding petitioner noted in the file, in addition to a final note stating quote “terminated, no sales, 
driving AWOL, bad reviews, no rehire”. (Tr. 164). (Rx1) Mr. Allgood testified he had never seen 
so many infractions happen that quickly. He stated that petitioner had been driving the work 
vehicle after hours with passengers, which was against policy, as late as midnight. Petitioner was 
also parking the vehicle at unapproved addresses, which was also against company policy. (Tr. 
164). The company policy was to park the vehicle at the address given on the application. (Id.)  
 
Mr. Allgood testified that he discussed the above infractions with the petitioner, got into a verbal 
altercation and terminated him on February 12, 2025. He believed this occurred around 10:30PM. 
(Tr. 165). Mr. Allgood explained that he recalled this conversation because there was a woman in 
the passenger seat of the company vehicle whom he was able to see via the dashcams in the vehicle 
that was also screaming at him and that he could see them eating in the vehicle. (Tr. 165).  He 
testified that the safety features were disabled in the vehicle, which is how petitioner was able to 
use the vehicle after hours. He explained that there is a USB port that plugs into the GPS tracking 
device that is attached to the disabler, which was cut. (Tr. 166). Mr. Allgood testified that petitioner 
became upset when learning of his termination and stated “it wasn’t his fault and he had to bring 
the vehicle to get something to eat and it was not normally something he would do.” (Tr. 167) In

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
 
The Arbitrator adopts the Findings of Fact in support of the Conclusions of law set forth below.  
To obtain compensation under the Act, Petitioner has the burden of proving, by a preponderance 
of the evidence, all of the elements of his claim O’Dette v. Industrial Comm’n, 79 Ill. 2d 249, 
253 (1980) including that there is some causal relationship between his employment and his 
injury. Caterpillar Tractor Co. v. Industrial Comm’n, 129 Ill. 2d 52, 63 (1989). Credibility is the 
quality of a witness which renders his evidence worthy of belief.  The Arbitrator, whose province 
it is to evaluate witness credibility, evaluates the demeanor of the witness and any external 
inconsistencies with his/her testimony.  Where a claimant’s testimony is inconsistent with his/her 
actual behavior and conduct, the Commission has held that an award cannot stand.  McDonald v. 
Industrial Commission, 39 Ill. 2d 396 (1968); Swift v. Industrial Commission, 52 Ill. 2d 490 
(1972).  The Arbitrator, as the trier of fact in this case, has the responsibility to observe the 
witnesses testify, judge their credibility, and determine how much weight to afford their 
testimony and the other evidence presented. Walker v. Chicago Housing Authority, 2015 IL App 
(1st) 133788, ¶ 47. Internal inconsistencies in a claimant’s testimony, as well as conflicts between 
the claimant’s testimony and medical records, may be taken to indicate unreliability.  Gilbert v. 
Martin & Bayley/Hucks, 08 ILWC 004187 (2010). 
 
In the case at hand, the Arbitrator observed Petitioner during the hearing and does not find him to 
be an entirely credible witness. The Arbitrator finds Petitioner’s testimony to be inconsistent with 
all of the evidence record presented and finds petitioner to be an unreliable historian. The 
Arbitrator further finds the testimony of Mr. Allgood to be the most credible and most persuasive 
in this case for the reasons set forth below. Mr. Allgood was a more thorough historian that gave 
detailed and persuasive testimony regarding dates, times, content of conversations, etc. 
Respondent’s former employee, Mr. Worcester, also testified on behalf of Petitioner. This witness 
was generally credible but did not appear to have all of the facts, nor was he privy to conversations 
between petitioner and respondent and was therefore not as reliable or persuasive as Mr. Allgood.  
 
Issue B, whether there an employee-employer relationship, the Arbitrator finds as follows:  
 
To receive benefits under the Illinois Workers’ Compensation Act, petitioner must establish an 
employer-employee relationship at the time of the alleged work accident. Section 1(b)(2) of the 
Act defines an employee as “[e]very person in the service of another under any contract of hire, 
express or implied, oral or written.”  820 ILCS 305/1(b)(2) (West 2020).   
 
In this case, Respondent agrees Petitioner was briefly employed by Respondent, however 
Respondent denies the employee-employer relationship as of the date of Petitioner’s alleged motor 
vehicle accident on 2/14/25. Specifically, Respondent asserts and Mr. Allgood testified that he 
terminated petitioner on 2/12/25 around 10:30PM during their phone conversation.  
 
26IWCC0137

12 
 
The testimony shows Petitioner was most recently hired by respondent on February 8, 2025. (Tr. 
155). However, after multiple infractions over the course of four working days, petitioner was 
terminated by Respondent on February 12, 2025 per Mr. Allgood. (RX 1). Mr. Allgood, who 
handled customer relations for respondent, testified to the specific infractions incurred by 
petitioner during his employment with respondent through February 12, 2025.  These infractions 
were also documented in respondent’s service manager software, which would automatically 
populate customer complaints relating to a specific technician. (Tr. 158).  Regarding February 12, 
2025, Mr. Allgood testified regarding a notation in the software file for petitioner, which states 
“terminated, no sales, driving AWOL, bad reviews, no rehire.” (Tr. 164).   
 
The record and testimony show Petitioner was involved in a motor vehicle accident on February 
14, 2025. The Arbitrator however has been persuaded by the testimony of Mr. Allgood and 
supporting evidence (Rx1) that Petitioner was previously terminated by respondent on February 
12, 2025 via Mr. Allgood and was therefore not employed by Respondent on the alleged accident 
date of February 14, 2025.   
 
Petitioner testified that he was never made aware that he was terminated at any point prior to 
February 14, 2025. (Tr. 50).  This testimony is contradicted by both respondent’s software 
system’s entry from February 12, 2025 (Tr. 164), and by the testimony of Jonathan Allgood, who 
was very convincing in his testimony and specifically recalled the details and circumstances of his 
February 12, 2025 conversation with petitioner communicating the termination.  (Tr. 165). This is 
unlike petitioner who on multiple occasions during testimony, did not remember who he spoke 
with or was in contact with, when allegedly communicating with respondent.  
 
The Arbitrator believes Mr. Allgood’s testimony to be most likely and believable and finds it 
reasonable that Petitioner became upset during the termination call with Allgood and responded to 
him by asking if he would still be reimbursed for his gas expenses (Tr. 167).  The Arbitrator notes 
Petitioner’s Exhibit H details petitioner apologizing for raising his voice prior and instructions by 
respondent to return the company vehicle to the mechanic shop (PX H). 
 
The Arbitrator notes compensation has been denied in instances where the claimant’s credibility 
was suspect. Petitioner in this matter has shown he is both not a reliable narrator and is not credible 
as to the details and events predicating his claim for benefits under the Act. Petitioner consistently 
asserted that he could not recall whom he spoke with from respondent. When asked who he spoke 
with about “upsales” from respondent, petitioner could not recall. (Tr. 18). Petitioner again could 
not remember whom he spoke with on the accident date of February 14, 2025. (Tr. 27).  After the 
collision, petitioner stated he let someone from respondent’s office know, who told him to continue 
to work, but he was again unable to remember whom he spoke with. (Tr. 36).   Petitioner also 
could not recall whom he spoke with from respondent regarding taking the vehicle for repairs or 
switching repair shops, despite these events occurring less than six months prior to trial.  
 
 
 
 
 
26IWCC0137

13 
 
The Arbitrator further finds the testimony from Jonathan Allgood to be more credible and 
persuasive than that of Benjamin Worcester regarding the events leading up to petitioner’s motor 
vehicle accident on February 14, 2025.  The individual instructed by respondent via Mr. Allgood 
to assist Mr. Worcester with his work vehicle on February 14, 2025 was a well-known and 
frequently used mechanic named Dale, who lived nearby to Mr. Worcester, a mere 6 blocks away 
(Tr. 175). Mr. Allgood testified he believed Mr. Worcester was talking about Dale not Petitioner 
when Mr. Worcester communicated with him on the date of the accident.  
 
 The Arbitrator must also note that Mr. Worcester had a long history with respondent that ended 
with a contentious termination, and ongoing legal matter/claim, which can impact his impartiality 
and overall credibility and persuasiveness as witness in this matter. In addition, Mr. Worcester was 
not a supervisor to petitioner and was not involved in the hiring or firing of employees, and was 
not involved in the conversations between Petitioner and Mr. Allgood and/or respondent. He did 
not have the whole story and did not have all the facts as it relates to the employment relationship 
Petitioner had or did not have with respondent. Clearly, Petitioner did not inform Mr. Worcester 
of his conversation with Mr. Allgood, nor did he tell Mr. Worcester that he was terminated before 
the accident. Mr. Allgood in contrast, was in direct contact with petitioner and had first hand 
knowledge as to petitioner’s infractions, his use and/or misuse of the company vehicle and his 
actions post termination on 2/12/25, including the disabling or cutting of the starter-disabler and 
eventually cutting/disabling of the GPS.  
 
Petitioner’s use of respondent’s vehicle after his termination on February 12, 2025 was not 
authorized by respondent as testified to Mr. Allgood.  Evidence of petitioner’s unauthorized use 
of the vehicle following February 12, 2025 includes petitioner’s subsequent tampering with the 
starter-disabler and the GPS tracking system installed in the vehicle which had to be repaired (Tr. 
197). Mr. Allgood explained even on the date of the termination 2/12/25, Petitioner was driving 
the vehicle late at night without permission and getting food with a woman in the work van, who 
he actually saw via dash cams during the conversation. The Arbitrator notes that Petitioner would 
not have been able to drive the vehicle at the time of the conversation above if he had not already 
disabled or cut the starter-disabler because Petitioner did not have permission to be driving the 
vehicle late at night to get food or to have non employees in the vehicle. There were also no jobs 
listed on the employee log (Rx1) after the termination as well.  
 
The Arbitrator finds that once petitioner disabled or cut the safety features to operate the vehicle, 
he was using the work van for personal use.  Despite the above, when asked on cross-examination 
if at any time, he had disabled the security features in the company vehicle, petitioner still stated 
he had not. (Tr. 92). Per the evidence presented, Petitioner was the sole driver of and in possession 
of this We Clean Carpet van. He brought it home each night and there is not testimony or evidence 
of anyone else having access to this vehicle other than Mr. Worcester. The Arbitrator finds that 
Petitioner would have been the only person to have cut or disabled the starter disabler and 
eventually GPS. Mr. Worcester was also not aware that the starter disabler and or GPS had been 
tampered with. Therefore, Petitioner’s testimony is not viewed to be entirely credible based on the 
above and the Arbitrator is not persuaded by Petitioner in his denial at trial that he was ever 
terminated on 2/12/25 and before his motor vehicle accident on 2/14/25.

In comparison, per the credible testimony of Mr. Allgood, petitioner then continued to drive the 
vehicle for days for personal use, following both the termination on 2/12/25 and the car accident

Based upon the entire record and the above analysis, the Arbitrator finds an employee-employer 
relationship did not exist between Petitioner and Respondent on the date of accident of February

Issue G, petitioner’s earnings, the Arbitrator finds as follows:   
 
Petitioner was told to report into work for respondent on February 8, 2025. (Tr. 155). The record 
shows he was only employed with Respondent for approximately four days total prior to his 
termination on February 12, 2025.  
26IWCC0137

15 
 
 
Cleaning technicians for Respondent are paid on commission. This is based on the amount of work 
completed and jobs done. (Tr. 147). Respondent confirmed that every technician gets 20% of each 
dispatched job and up to 50% of any additional services they provide to customers when they are 
on location. (Tr. 147). Respondent charged $89.00 per job per Mr. Allgood. (Tr. 148). However 
the We Clean Carpet pay scale document which was not deemed to be a false or fraudulent 
document by respondent, reflected the pay of 20% per each job and provided a job rate of $95.00 
(PxE). Thus using the pay document, 20% of $95.00 resulted in a $19.00 payment per job for the 
technicians. Technicians would complete an average of three jobs per day, with 4 jobs per day and 
24 jobs per week as the goal.  
 
Technicians could also earn more based on extra services rendered at each job assignment. For 
these additional services, technicians would receive up to 50% of the extra services rendered. (Tr. 
149). If no additional services were rendered, then the technician would not receive any additional 
compensation. Technicians were asked to work Monday through Saturday and would aim for 24 
jobs per week, but most averaged 18 to 20. (Tr. 150). Using a pay rate of $57.00 per day, multiplied 
by working 6 days a week, results in a base pay of $342.00 per week without additional 
compensation added.  
 
Petitioner introduced into evidence a We Clean Carpet pay scale document which shows cleaning 
technicians would make approximately $1,218 per week working 6 days per week and completing 
4 jobs per day. (PxE) Petitioner only worked for Respondent for four days and averaged $40.00 
per workday.  (Tr. 150). While Mr. Worcester also testified that in his 14 years, the average 
paycheck would be $1000 and would range from $700-1,500 dependent on the season. However, 
Mr. Worcester testified that during his week with Petitioner, they only completed 12-18 jobs per 
week which further evidences that Petitioner was not near the average goal of 24 jobs per week 
plus upsales, to warrant the $1,218 weekly wage that was shown on the pay document.  In his short 
time with Respondent, he only completed four jobs on his own. (Tr. 155). Petitioner failed to 
complete the additional services requested by customers and needed to be retrained on providing 
additional services/upsales. (Tr. 160).  
 
Based on the jobs petitioner completed in his short time with petitioner and because the upsale or 
additional service upgrade bonuses are not guaranteed, the Arbitrator finds it reasonable that the 
average weekly wage be based on a 3 job per day and 6 days per week rate. Respondent charged 
$89.00-95.00 per job and the Arbitrator will rely on the PxE estimated pay amounts. 20% of $95.00 
was $19.00 per job. At a pay rate of $57.00 per day (assuming 3 jobs per day), this results in a base 
pay and average weekly wage of $342.00 for Petitioner.  Based upon the foregoing, the Arbitrator 
finds an average weekly wage of $342.00.
